text: Exuberance is enthusiasm with the brakes off — bubbling, high-spirited excitement that pushes people further than a cool head would go. In markets the word is almost technical, thanks to Alan Greenspan’s 1996 warning about “irrational exuberance”: buyers whose eagerness has outrun the facts. Saying exuberance still reigns over the doll market is the writer’s way of noting that prices here are still set by mood rather than arithmetic.

An adage is a short saying repeated so long that it passes for wisdom, like “practice makes perfect”. The word hints at both age and untested authority — an adage is what people say, not what anyone has proved. The traders’ adage quoted here, that bull markets are murdered by central banks, is set up precisely so the writer can point out that this one was murdered by a toy company instead.

Embezzlement is stealing money that was entrusted to your care — the treasurer quietly moving club funds into a personal account, rather than a burglar taking the cash box. That trust is what separates it from plain theft, and from fraud, which works by talking someone into handing the money over. The article says this mania produced counterfeit dolls instead of embezzlement, meaning the swindling happened in factories rather than in company accounts.

Labubu is a collectable toy character — a snaggle-toothed elf-like creature sold by the Chinese company Pop Mart, usually in sealed “blind boxes” where you do not know which figure you are getting. The dolls became a global craze, sold as keychain charms and, at the top end, in four-foot versions. The article treats the hunger for them as a speculative mania rather than a toy story.

Pop Mart is the Chinese toy company that makes Labubus, with shops in cities around the world including London. It is publicly listed, so anyone can buy its shares, and its share price stands at around half its August peak as the frenzy fades. The article’s sharpest point is that Pop Mart ended the Labubu resale boom itself, by manufacturing far more dolls.

A Lafufu is a counterfeit Labubu — a knock-off with a sloppy paint job and, often, the wrong number of teeth, since a genuine Labubu has nine. The name is a joke on the original. Fakes on this scale are one symptom of a mania: British officials seized £3.5m of fake toys in nine months, nine-tenths of them Lafufus.

In economics, a bubble is a run-up in the price of something far beyond any level the underlying facts could justify, kept going by buyers who expect to sell to someone even more eager. Famous ones include Dutch tulip bulbs in the 1630s and internet shares in the late 1990s, and they end when the supply of eager buyers runs out. The writer’s joke is that a doll has no underlying facts at all, which makes the word awkward to apply.

An asset is anything owned that has value and can be sold — shares, gold, a flat, a bond, and in this story a doll. Economists sort them into asset classes that behave differently, which is why the article warns that the laws of one asset class do not always apply to others. Treating a toy as an asset, bought to resell rather than to enjoy, is what turns collecting into speculation.

The fundamentals of an asset are the measurable facts about the real money it produces and the real things it owns: a company’s earnings, its cash flow, its dividends, its factories. Prices are supposed to bear some relation to them, so a share trading at a thousand times annual earnings is said to have broken away from its fundamentals. The problem the article keeps returning to is that a plush elf has no fundamentals whatsoever.

Earnings are the profit a company actually keeps over a period, usually a year — what is left of its sales once wages, materials, taxes and everything else are paid. Comparing a share price with annual earnings gives the price-to-earnings ratio, the quickest test of whether a share looks dear. Paying hundreds or thousands of times earnings, as the article describes, means paying today for centuries of future profit.

Cash flow is the actual money moving into and out of a business, as opposed to profit worked out on paper. Investors watch it because an asset that throws off cash can be valued by adding up the cash it will deliver over time. Gold, as the article notes, generates no cash flows at all, which is why valuing it is famously slippery — and a doll is a step worse again.

A store of value is something people hold because they expect it to keep its worth over time, rather than because it feeds them or pays them anything. Gold is the classic example, prized for millennia for exactly this reason, and storing value is one of the three jobs economists assign to money. The phrase is here to show that even an asset with no cash flows can have a serious reason for being held — a reason a Labubu lacks.

A share, also called a stock, is a slice of ownership in a company: own one and you own a fraction of whatever the business earns and owns. Shares change hands on stock exchanges at whatever price buyers and sellers agree, which is how Pop Mart’s share price can halve without the company doing anything that day. Nineteenth-century swindlers sold shares in railways that did not exist — the era’s version of a Lafufu.

Charles Kindleberger was an American economist best known for “Manias, Panics and Crashes” (1978), a history of financial bubbles that finds the same pattern repeating across centuries: easy money, a wave of greed, then swindlers arriving to feed on it. The book is still a standard reference on how bubbles behave. The article measures Labubumania against it and finds it follows the script, minus the financial wreckage.

Fraud is deceiving someone in order to take their money — inventing a business, faking the figures, selling what does not exist. It differs from embezzlement, where the money was handed to you legitimately first, and from counterfeiting, where the deception sits in the goods themselves. The article’s point is that this mania bred fakes rather than financial fraud.

A bull market is a long stretch of rising prices, named for the way a bull strikes upwards with its horns; a falling market is a bear market. Traders use the terms for shares, but here the writer applies them to dolls. The adage that bull markets are murdered by central banks refers to interest-rate rises, which make borrowing costly and cool the buying.

A central bank is the public institution that manages a country’s money — the Federal Reserve in America, the Bank of England in Britain — setting interest rates and standing behind the banking system. When it raises rates, borrowing becomes dearer and speculative buying usually subsides, which is the sense of the adage quoted here. Nobody at a central bank had anything to do with Labubus, which is the joke.

The secondary market is where things are traded between owners after the original sale: the resale ticket site, the sneaker app, the stock exchange where shares bought at flotation change hands. The maker receives none of that money, which is why a resale price can drift far above the shop price whenever supply is tight. Pop Mart flattened the Labubu secondary market simply by making ten times as many dolls.

A mark-up is the amount added to what something cost you, to arrive at what you sell it for. Resellers live on mark-ups, and a mark-up survives only while buyers cannot easily get the thing at its normal price. Once 30m plush toys a month were leaving the factories, the Labubu mark-up had nothing left to rest on.

Scalpers buy scarce things — concert tickets, trainers, limited-run dolls — purely to resell them at a higher price to people who missed out. The word is usually thrown as an insult, though scalpers argue they are simply carrying the risk of holding stock nobody may want. The article expects a few of them to lose money as Labubu prices fall, with no wider damage.

An aesthetic is a style or look — the overall visual flavour of a thing — and the word also names the branch of philosophy concerned with beauty and taste. Calling something someone’s aesthetic has become ordinary in fashion and online. Here it captures the deliberate Labubu combination of cute and sinister: a baby elf with sharpened teeth.

To sport something is to wear or display it openly, with a touch of pride — nothing to do with games. It carries a faint swagger: you sport a new haircut or a team scarf, you do not sport an ordinary coat. Labubu fans sport the dolls on keychains, hanging them where they will be seen.

Speculation is buying something not to use it but to sell it on at a higher price, accepting real risk of loss for the chance of a quick gain. It shades into investing, but an investor expects the asset itself to earn something, while a speculator only needs the next buyer to pay more. Calling Labubu-buying speculative marks the moment the doll stopped being a toy and became a bet.

A mania is a frenzy of collective enthusiasm that carries people past their own judgement; the adjective manic describes that same restless, overheated state. In finance the word is standard, as in the Dutch tulip mania or the title of Kindleberger’s book. The article’s verdict is that things are now less manic than they were last summer.

Euphoric describes an intense, sometimes unrealistic feeling of joy and confidence, the mood in which everything seems certain to go right. Traders described as euphoric are the ones pushing prices up without checking what they are buying. Euphoria is the emotional engine of a bubble, and its evaporation is what ends one.

Underlying means lying beneath the surface and giving rise to what you can see — the underlying cause of an argument, the underlying facts of a business. In finance it points at the real economics beneath a price: a company’s underlying annual earnings, as opposed to whatever its shares happen to trade at today. The gap between price and underlying value is the whole subject of this article.

To prize something is to value it highly and want to keep it, so a prized object is one treated as precious. It has nothing to do with winning a prize, or with prising a lid off. Gold, the article says, has been prized as a store of value for millennia despite producing nothing.

To wax is to grow, increase or become — an old use that survives in wax and wane, and in waxing lyrical. Individuals who wax greedy are people becoming greedier, not people polishing anything. Kindleberger reaches for the old-fashioned verb to give his description of a boom the flavour of a timeless pattern.

A swindler cheats people out of their money by deception, usually with charm and a plausible story rather than force. Kindleberger’s point is that swindlers are not an accident of booms but a dependable feature of them, because greed creates the opening. The swindler of the 1800s sold shares in imaginary railways; today’s sells a Lafufu.

Scarce means there is not enough of something to go round at the current price, which is the precondition for anyone paying over the odds. Scarcity is the foundation of every resale trade, and it can be manufactured — a limited run, a weekly raffle, a queue outside the shop. When Pop Mart made Labubus plentiful, the scarcity holding up resale prices vanished.

Rabid means fanatical and uncontrolled, borrowed from rabies, the disease that leaves an animal frantic. Applied to people it is unflattering: a rabid fan has lost all perspective. Rabid speculation means buying driven by frenzy rather than by any judgement of what the thing is worth.

In finance, returns are the gains an investment produces — the profit, dividends or rise in price you collect for putting your money in. The word has nothing to do with going back, or with taking goods back to a shop. Investors want persistent, reliable returns, which is exactly what a toy craze cannot promise.

Your correspondent is how a reporter refers to themselves in print without saying I — a convention The Economist keeps because its articles carry no bylines. It signals a personal observation rather than a reported fact. Here it flags an opinion: the writer cannot see why anyone would pay even a tenth of £850 for the doll.

Something described as a steal is a bargain, priced far below what it is worth — nobody has stolen anything. The joke here is comparative: a doll at £850 counts as a steal only beside one that fetched $150,000. English makes the same move with a snip and a bargain.

Out of whack means out of proper alignment or proportion — informal, and common in American English for anything that has drifted from where it should be. Prices out of whack with fundamentals are prices that no longer match the underlying facts. You can just as easily say your sleep schedule is out of whack.

To bid up a price is to drive it higher by competing to buy, the way rival bidders at an auction push a lot past its estimate. It describes a price rising because of eagerness among buyers, not because the thing itself got any better. Euphoric traders bidding up a company’s value is the mechanism by which a bubble inflates.

By a factor of ten means multiplied by ten, not increased by ten — the standard way of saying how many times larger something has become. Expanding production by a factor of ten took Pop Mart to around 30m plush toys a month. The same phrasing turns up constantly in science writing: brighter by a factor of a hundred, faster by a factor of a thousand.

Raison d’être is French for reason for being, used in English for the single purpose that justifies something’s existence. When the article says the secondary market lost its raison d’être, it means the whole point of that trade — buying scarce dolls to sell them on dear — had gone. It is pronounced roughly ray-ZON DET-ruh.

A knock-on effect is a consequence that spreads outward from an event to things not directly involved, like one falling domino toppling the next. The phrase is common in British English; Americans more often say ripple effect. A bursting bubble in shares can knock on into banks, jobs and pensions, whereas a bursting bubble in dolls mostly does not.

To lose your shirt is to lose almost everything you have on a bad bet or investment — the image is of being stripped down to nothing. It is used for heavy personal losses, not for an ordinary business setback. A few scalpers losing their shirts is the article’s estimate of the total damage from this bubble.
